slides.title: Can this really work?
slides.text: Caps are promises. This story shows the cryptography that keeps them: which keys exist, what each step does to them, and the few things no cryptography can do.

slides.title: Four kinds of keys.
slides.text: Each one has exactly one job.
list: Seal: signs a piece of data's first rule, then is destroyed.
Identity key: a lock only you can open, grown from your passkey.
Role key: a lock all members of a role can open.
Data key: the key the data itself is encrypted with.

slides.title: Data is born.
slides.text: Your device makes a fresh seal. Its public half becomes the data's ID. It signs the first rule, and the private half is wiped. From now on, the rules can only change through someone the rules allow.

slides.title: Reading is a chain of envelopes.
slides.text: The content is encrypted with the data key. The data key sits in an {envelope} for every role that may read. The role key sits in an envelope for every member. Your identity key opens the first envelope, and the chain opens the rest.

slides.title: Writing is a chain of signatures.
slides.text: Mia ticks “buy milk”. Her signer signs the change. Every device that receives it checks three links before merging: the signer acts for Mia, Mia is in “home”, and “home” has update on this list. One broken link, and the change is dropped.

slides.title: Adding Mia to a role: one envelope.
slides.text: An admin of the role puts the role key in an envelope for Mia's identity key. That's all. Mia can now read everything the role can read, including what came before she joined.

slides.title: Giving a cap: read needs a key, the rest needs a rule.
slides.text: Giving “plumber” read on the tap item puts the item's data key in an envelope for the plumber role. Giving update needs no key at all: it's a signed rule in the item's history, and every device enforces it.

slides.title: Removing someone means new keys.
slides.text: The plumber still knows the old role key. So the role gets a new one, in envelopes for the remaining members only. Every piece of data the role reads gets a new data key the next time it changes. This is {rotation}: the plumber keeps the past, and loses the future.
flow: new data key on next change

slides.title: Taking a cap away.
slides.text: Taking update away is just a new rule. Taking read away rotates the data key, and the new one goes to every reading role except that one.

slides.title: Losing your phone.
slides.text: Your identity named its next signer when it was born, so you can switch to it. Then your identity key rotates too, and your other device puts your role keys into envelopes for the new key. The lost phone opens nothing new.

slides.title: Two things at once.
slides.text: Mia edits the list on a train, offline, at the same moment you remove her. When both devices meet, the removal wins: her edit is dropped everywhere. Every device applies the same rule, so they all end up agreeing.

slides.title: What no cryptography can do.
list: Make someone unsee what they already read.
Hide part of a piece of data from a reader: read is per piece of data, so small things you share alone are their own data.
Stop a reader from copying what they can read.

slides.title: The whole machine.
list: Data is born with a seal that is used once and destroyed.
Read is a chain of envelopes: identity key, role key, data key.
Every other op is a chain of signatures, checked by every device.
Removing someone rotates keys: they keep the past and lose the future.
